params.prompt: Every marketplace plan covers the same essential health benefits; the metal level tells you how the cost is split. Actuarial value is the share of covered costs the plan pays for a standard population. Bronze plans pay about sixty percent, silver about seventy, gold about eighty and platinum about ninety. Lower metals mean lower premiums and higher deductibles. Catastrophic plans, with very high deductibles, are limited to people under thirty or those with a hardship exemption. Marcus’s daughter, turning twenty-six and healthy, might pick bronze; Rosa, who expects a surgery, might pick gold.

Maryland Health Connection runs the state’s individual Exchange and a Small Business Health Options Program, or S H O P, for employers with up to fifty employees. In S H O P the employer picks a contribution level and one or more plans, employees enroll, and the employer receives a single consolidated bill and pays it; the marketplace or its administrator distributes premiums to the carriers. Enrollment may run through an authorized producer. Employers with fewer than twenty-five full-time equivalent employees and modest average wages may qualify for the small business health care tax credit, available only for coverage bought through S H O P, for two consecutive years.

When a plan denies a claim, refuses to authorize care or rescinds coverage, that is an adverse benefit determination, and the member may appeal. The first step is an internal appeal to the plan, requested within one hundred eighty days of the denial. The plan must have the appeal reviewed by someone not involved in the original decision and, for medical judgments, by an appropriate clinician. Decisions are due within thirty days for care not yet received and sixty days for care already received. Urgent cases get an expedited decision; Maryland requires emergency grievance decisions within twenty-four hours. The member may see the file and submit evidence.

If the plan upholds a denial based on medical necessity or similar judgment, the member may seek external review by an independent party. In Maryland, the Insurance Administration handles complaints about adverse decisions, obtains an independent medical review when needed, and its determination binds the carrier. The Attorney General’s Health Education and Advocacy Unit helps consumers file grievances and gather records. External review is free to the member and must be decided within set time limits, with expedited review for urgent care. A member may also skip the internal step when the carrier fails to follow its own process or the case is urgent.

People who buy through the individual Exchange may qualify for a premium tax credit based on household income relative to the federal poverty level. The credit is usually paid in advance directly to the insurer, lowering the monthly premium, and is reconciled on the tax return. It is not available to people offered affordable employer coverage or eligible for Medicaid; in Maryland, adults with income below one hundred thirty-eight percent of poverty generally qualify for Medicaid instead. Cost-sharing reductions lower deductibles and copayments for enrollees between one hundred and two hundred fifty percent of poverty, but only in silver plans. The income ranges and credit amounts are set by Congress and change, so check current figures.

The federal individual mandate penalty was reduced to zero beginning in two thousand nineteen, so an individual who goes without coverage owes no federal penalty, and Maryland imposes none; Maryland instead uses an Easy Enrollment checkbox on the state tax return to connect uninsured residents with coverage. Penalties remain for employers and insurers. An applicable large employer, one with fifty or more full-time equivalent employees, that fails to offer affordable minimum value coverage to its full-time employees can owe the employer shared responsibility payment. Insurers and group plans that violate A C A rules face federal excise taxes and state fines through the Insurance Administration.

Rosa, an electrician, injures her shoulder and can no longer climb or pull wire. She could manage a hardware store or estimate jobs from a desk. Is she disabled? The answer depends entirely on how her policy defines the word. Disability income insurance does not pay because a person is hurt; it pays because the person meets the policy’s definition of total or partial disability. Two policies with identical benefit amounts can produce opposite claim decisions on the same injury. Before quoting any disability policy, a producer reads the definition and explains it in the client’s own terms.

An own-occupation definition pays when the insured cannot perform the material and substantial duties of her regular occupation, even if she could work at something else. Under a true own-occupation policy Rosa is totally disabled the day she cannot work as an electrician, and she may earn income in another job while collecting full benefits. A modified own-occupation definition pays only if she is also not working elsewhere. Own-occupation coverage is the most favorable and the most expensive, and insurers reserve it for professionals and skilled trades with definable duties.

An any-occupation definition pays only when the insured cannot perform the duties of any occupation for which she is reasonably suited by education, training and experience. Rosa, able to manage a store, would not be totally disabled under this test. It is the strictest definition, resembles the Social Security standard, and costs the least. Many policies and most group long-term disability plans use a split definition: own occupation for the first two years, then any occupation. A producer must warn clients that benefits can end at the two-year mark if they could do other suitable work.

A third approach drops the occupational test. A pure loss of income, or income replacement, contract pays based on what the insured actually loses. If Rosa’s shoulder cuts her income from six thousand dollars a month to three thousand dollars, the policy pays a benefit proportional to the fifty percent loss, whether she stopped working or changed jobs. These contracts need no definition of total disability for most claims, because they measure dollars rather than duties. They suit self-employed people whose income varies and whose disability may be partial from the start. Lesson thirty shows the residual arithmetic in detail.

Some losses are so severe that the policy presumes total disability without applying the occupational test. The usual list is total and permanent loss of sight in both eyes, hearing in both ears, speech, or the use of two limbs. If Rosa loses both hands in an accident she is presumed totally disabled, benefits begin, often without the elimination period, and they continue for the full benefit period even if she later earns income. Presumptive disability is a floor that guarantees payment in the worst cases; everything short of the list still runs through the policy definition.

Policies require the insured to be under the regular care of a physician for the condition causing the disability. The requirement prevents claims for conditions nobody is treating and lets the insurer verify continuing disability through medical records and periodic proof. Most modern policies waive it when care would not improve the condition, so a paralyzed insured need not schedule pointless visits. Rosa must keep her orthopedic appointments while she claims, and her physician’s reports will support each monthly benefit. Put the pieces together: definition met, care maintained, elimination period served, benefit paid.
